steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our optimization paper on stable nonconvex-nonconcave training via linear interpolation: why Lookahead-style interpolation stabilizes training, the cohypomonotone setting and open questions about last-iterate rates, how our RAPP method and the Krasnosel'skii-Mann view answer them, and a list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Stability in training; Lookahead as a heuristic
2. What stability means and why it is hard to analyze
3. Global convergence under cohypomonotonicity
4. Existing methods (EG+, EG, implicit schemes) and open questions
5. Scope: 1-SCLI schemes vs Halpern-type methods
6. Linear interpolation / KM iteration as the unifying mechanism
7. Contributions

- EG: last iterate only under mild cohypomonotonicity, only unconstrained (cite)
- recent: last iterate rates for same (tight) range as EG+ best iterate, but implicit scheme, complexity blows up with cohypomonotonicity (cite)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Stability is a major concern when large scale models are trained. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) in particular are known to be notoriously difficult to train. The Lookahead algorithm was recently proposed for GANs to stabilize training, and it linearly interpolates with a slow moving iterate. This mechanism has had superior empirical performance in both minimization and minimax problems, but it is still mostly a heuristic without much theoretical motivation.

A major obstacle to treating it theoretically is capturing the (fuzzy) notion of stability. Roughly speaking, in practice a training dynamics is called unstable when the iterates either cycle indefinitely or (eventually) diverge, which has been observed for the Adam optimizer (see e.g. one study and another study respectively). On the other hand a stable dynamics has some bias towards stationary points. The notion of stability used so far (e.g. in prior work) is based on the spectral radius and so it is inherently local.

In this work we want to establish global convergence properties, and for that some structural assumptions are needed. One (nonmonotone) structure that is well suited to studying stability is cohypomonotonicity, studied in earlier work, because even the extragradient method has been shown to cycle and diverge in this problem class (see one work and another respectively). Figure 1 gives a geometric intuition for these difficulties. Biasing the optimization schemes towards stationary points becomes a central concern, and in Figure 2 we show that Lookahead can indeed converge for such nonmonotone problems.

The extragradient+ algorithm (EG+) proposed by prior work is a principled approach to cohypomonotone problems. But the only known rates are for the best iterate, which can be problematic to pick in practice. It is not clear if last iterate rates for EG+ are possible even in the monotone case (see the discussion before Thm. 3.3 in another paper). So the community has instead shown last iterate results for the extragradient (EG) method, even though it was originally developed for the monotone case. Maybe not surprisingly, EG only has a last iterate guarantee under a mild form of cohypomonotonicity, and it has only been studied in the unconstrained case. Recently last iterate rates were established for the same (tight) range of cohypomonotone problems where EG+ has best iterate guarantees. But the scheme that was analyzed is implicit and its complexity blows up as cohypomonotonicity increases. So the questions are: Can an explicit scheme have last iterate rates for the same range of cohypomonotone problems? Can the rate be agnostic to the degree of cohypomonotonicity? We answer yes to both.

5. Scope
- 1-SCLI schemes: update depends only on previous iterate, time-invariant
- alternative: Halpern-type methods, explicit scheme for cohypomonotone problems, constrained extension

6. KM iteration
- linear interpolation (as in Lookahead) is principled mechanism for convergence here
- = Krasnosel'skii-Mann (KM) iteration in nonexpansive operator theory
- EG+, our relaxed approximate proximal point method (RAPP), Lookahead-based algorithms = (inexact) KM iteration; simple proofs in cohypomonotone case

7. Contributions
- RAPP: global last iterate rates, constrained and regularized settings; first 1-SCLI scheme with non-asymptotic guarantees for \rho -comonotone, \rho>-\nicefrac{{1}}{{2L}}; byproduct: implicit scheme rate independent of cohypomonotonicity; monotonic decrease of operator norm (not possible for EG+); RAPP = EG+ with multiple extrapolation steps
- RAPP inner routine -> GDA / EG: rediscover Lookahead algorithms; nonexpansive base optimizers; optimal \lambda=0.5 = default in practice
- \tau=2: LA-GDA = interpolation between GDA and EG+; convergence for \rho>-\nicefrac{{1}}{{3\sqrt{3}L}}; large \tau counterexample; propose LA-CEG+ for \rho>-\nicefrac{{1}}{{2L}}
- experiments: synthetic examples and GAN training; stabilizing effect; RAPP similar benefit to Lookahead
- overview in Table 1

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Stability is a major concern when large scale models are trained. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) in particular are known to be notoriously difficult to train. The Lookahead algorithm was recently proposed for GANs to stabilize training, and it linearly interpolates with a slow moving iterate. This mechanism has had superior empirical performance in both minimization and minimax problems, but it is still mostly a heuristic without much theoretical motivation.

A major obstacle to treating it theoretically is capturing the (fuzzy) notion of stability. Roughly speaking, in practice a training dynamics is called unstable when the iterates either cycle indefinitely or (eventually) diverge, which has been observed for the Adam optimizer (see e.g. one study and another study respectively). On the other hand a stable dynamics has some bias towards stationary points. The notion of stability used so far (e.g. in prior work) is based on the spectral radius and so it is inherently local.

In this work we want to establish global convergence properties, and for that some structural assumptions are needed. One (nonmonotone) structure that is well suited to studying stability is cohypomonotonicity, studied in earlier work, because even the extragradient method has been shown to cycle and diverge in this problem class (see one work and another respectively). Figure 1 gives a geometric intuition for these difficulties. Biasing the optimization schemes towards stationary points becomes a central concern, and in Figure 2 we show that Lookahead can indeed converge for such nonmonotone problems.

The extragradient+ algorithm (EG+) proposed by prior work is a principled approach to cohypomonotone problems. But the only known rates are for the best iterate, which can be problematic to pick in practice. It is not clear if last iterate rates for EG+ are possible even in the monotone case (see the discussion before Thm. 3.3 in another paper). So the community has instead shown last iterate results for the extragradient (EG) method, even though it was originally developed for the monotone case. Maybe not surprisingly, EG only has a last iterate guarantee under a mild form of cohypomonotonicity, and it has only been studied in the unconstrained case. Recently last iterate rates were established for the same (tight) range of cohypomonotone problems where EG+ has best iterate guarantees. But the scheme that was analyzed is implicit and its complexity blows up as cohypomonotonicity increases. So the questions are: Can an explicit scheme have last iterate rates for the same range of cohypomonotone problems? Can the rate be agnostic to the degree of cohypomonotonicity? We answer yes to both.

This work focuses on 1-SCLI schemes, where the update rule only depends on the previous iterate in a time-invariant way. Another approach to last iterate results is Halpern-type methods, with an explicit scheme developed in one work for cohypomonotone problems and later extended to the constrained case in another.

As will become clear, the linear interpolation that is also used in Lookahead is a principled mechanism behind convergence in this nonmonotone class. In the theory of nonexpansive operators this iterative interpolation is more broadly called the Krasnosel'skiĭ-Mann (KM) iteration. We show that the extragradient+ algorithm (EG+), our proposed relaxed approximate proximal point method (RAPP), and Lookahead based algorithms are all instances of the (inexact) KM iteration, and we give simple proofs for these schemes in the cohypomonotone case.

Our contributions are the following:

- 1. We prove global convergence rates for the last iterate of our proposed algorithm RAPP, which also handles constrained and regularized settings. This makes RAPP the first 1-SCLI scheme with non-asymptotic guarantees for \rho -comonotone problems that only requires \rho>-\nicefrac{{1}}{{2L}}. As a byproduct we get a last iterate convergence rate for an implicit scheme that does not depend on the degree of cohypomonotonicity. We establish the last iterate rates by showing that the operator norm decreases monotonically, which is not possible for EG+. This contrast is maybe surprising, because RAPP can be seen as an extension of EG+ that just takes multiple extrapolation steps.

- 2. If we replace the inner optimization routine in RAPP with gradient descent ascent (GDA) and extragradient (EG) we rediscover the Lookahead algorithms that were considered in earlier work. We get guarantees for the Lookahead variants by deriving nonexpansive properties of the base optimizers. Casting Lookahead as a KM iteration, we find that the optimal interpolation constant is \lambda=0.5. This is the default value used in practice for both minimization and minimax, so this gives theoretical motivation for the parameter value.

- 3. For \tau=2 inner iterations we see that LA-GDA reduces to a linear interpolation between GDA and EG+, and this lets us get global convergence in \rho -comonotone problems when \rho>-\nicefrac{{1}}{{3\sqrt{3}L}}. But for \tau large we give a counterexample that shows LA-GDA cannot be guaranteed to converge. So we instead propose LA-CEG+, which corrects the inner optimization to guarantee global convergence for \rho -comonotone problems when \rho>-\nicefrac{{1}}{{2L}}.

- 4. We test the methods on a suite of synthetic examples and on GAN training, and we confirm the stabilizing effect. Interestingly RAPP seems to give a similar benefit as Lookahead, which suggests that linear interpolation could play a key role experimentally too.

Table 1 gives an overview of the theoretical results.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Stability is a major concern when training large scale models. In particular, generative adversarial networks (GANs) are known to be notoriously difficult to train. To stabilize training, the Lookahead algorithm of [1] was recently proposed for GANs [2], which linearly interpolates with a slow moving iterate. The mechanism has enjoyed superior empirical performance in both minimization and minimax problems, but it remains largely a heuristic with little theoretical motivation.

One major obstacle to a theoretical treatment is capturing the (fuzzy) notion of stability. Loosely speaking, a training dynamics is referred to as unstable in practice when the iterates either cycle indefinitely or (eventually) diverge, as has been observed for the Adam optimizer (see e.g. [3] and [2] respectively). Conversely, a stable dynamics has some bias towards stationary points. The notion of stability so far (e.g. in [2]) is based on the spectral radius and is thus inherently local.

In this work, we are interested in establishing global convergence properties, which requires some structural assumptions. One (nonmonotone) structure that lends itself well to the study of stability is cohypomonotonicity, studied in [6,7], since even the extragradient method has been shown to cycle and diverge in this problem class (see [8] and [9] respectively). We provide a geometric intuition behind these difficulties in Figure 1. Biasing the optimization schemes towards stationary points becomes a central concern, and we demonstrate in Figure 2 that Lookahead can indeed converge for such nonmonotone problems.

A principled approach to cohypomonotone problems is the extragradient+ algorithm (EG+) proposed by [7]. However, the only known rates are on the best iterate, which can be problematic to pick in practice, and it is unclear whether last iterate rates for EG+ are possible even in the monotone case (see the discussion prior to Thm. 3.3 in [10]). For this reason, the community has instead resorted to showing last iterate results for the extragradient (EG) method of [11], despite it originally being developed for the monotone case. Maybe not surprisingly, EG only enjoys a last iterate guarantee under a mild form of cohypomonotonicity and has so far only been studied in the unconstrained case [12,4]. Recently, last iterate rates were established for the same (tight) range of cohypomonotone problems for which EG+ has best iterate guarantees. However, the analyzed scheme is implicit and its complexity blows up with increasing cohypomonotonicity [4]. This leaves two questions: Can an explicit scheme enjoy last iterate rates for the same range of cohypomonotone problems? Can the rate be agnostic to the degree of cohypomonotonicity? We answer both in the affirmative.

This work focuses on 1-SCLI schemes [13,14], whose update rule depends only on the previous iterate in a time-invariant fashion. Another approach to establishing last iterate results is Halpern-type methods, with an explicit scheme developed in [15] for cohypomonotone problems and later extended to the constrained case in [16] (cf.).

As will become clear, a principled mechanism behind convergence in this nonmonotone class is the linear interpolation also used in Lookahead. This iterative interpolation is more broadly referred to as the Krasnosel'skiĭ-Mann (KM) iteration in the theory of nonexpansive operators. We show that the extragradient+ algorithm (EG+) of [7], our proposed relaxed approximate proximal point method (RAPP), and Lookahead based algorithms are all instances of the (inexact) KM iteration, and we provide simple proofs for these schemes in the cohypomonotone case.

More concretely, we make the following contributions:

- 1. We prove global convergence rates for the last iterate of our proposed algorithm RAPP, which additionally handles constrained and regularized settings. This makes RAPP the first 1-SCLI scheme to have non-asymptotic guarantees for \rho -comonotone problems while only requiring \rho>-\nicefrac{{1}}{{2L}}. As a byproduct, we obtain a last iterate convergence rate for an implicit scheme that is independent of the degree of cohypomonotonicity. The last iterate rates are established by showing monotonic decrease of the operator norm, something which is not possible for EG+. This contrast is maybe surprising, since RAPP can be viewed as an extension of EG+ which simply takes multiple extrapolation steps.

- 2. By replacing the inner optimization routine in RAPP with gradient descent ascent (GDA) and extragradient (EG), we rediscover the Lookahead algorithms considered in [2]. We obtain guarantees for the Lookahead variants by deriving nonexpansive properties of the base optimizers. By casting Lookahead as a KM iteration, we find that the optimal interpolation constant is \lambda=0.5. This choice corresponds to the default value used in practice for both minimization and minimax, thus providing theoretical motivation for the parameter value.

- 3. For \tau=2 inner iterations, we observe that LA-GDA reduces to a linear interpolation between GDA and EG+, which allows us to obtain global convergence in \rho -comonotone problems when \rho>-\nicefrac{{1}}{{3\sqrt{3}L}}. However, for large \tau, we provide a counterexample showing that LA-GDA cannot be guaranteed to converge. We therefore propose LA-CEG+, which corrects the inner optimization to guarantee global convergence for \rho -comonotone problems when \rho>-\nicefrac{{1}}{{2L}}.

- 4. We test the methods on a suite of synthetic examples and GAN training, where we confirm the stabilizing effect. Interestingly, RAPP seems to provide a similar benefit as Lookahead, which suggests that linear interpolation could play a key role experimentally as well.
